Describe a project where you used Python or R to analyze clinical, biomedical, or other complex health-related data. What was the research question, what data did you work with, and what analytical approach did you use?
checks.expected: At Columbia’s Zuckerman Institute, I worked on a biomedical imaging project asking how well self-supervised learning could denoise two-photon calcium-imaging data while preserving neuronal signal. The data included real calcium-imaging videos and synthetic imaging datasets built from real neuronal spatial footprints, simulated temporal traces, and controlled Gaussian noise. I used Python-based deep learning workflows to implement a four-direction spatial masking strategy, integrate it with PMD spatial-component selection, and evaluate ResNet, U-Net, and lightweight convolutional models. I compared spatial, temporal, and combined denoising approaches, ran ablations on receptive fields, normalization, losses, and training settings, and assessed reconstruction fidelity, temporal correlation, signal retention, and rank-selection trade-offs.

checks.label: Tell us about a project where you used NLP, large language models, or retrieval-augmented generation to extract or structure information from unstructured text. What techniques or tools did you use, and how did you evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the results?
checks.expected: In Columbia AI Alignment Club, I worked on a project evaluating when Qwen models withhold versus produce answers for known and unknown entities. It was not a production RAG system, but it directly involved structuring and validating LLM behavior from unstructured natural-language responses. I used Hugging Face and TransformerLens, activation hooks across transformer layers, linear probes, feature-attribution graphs, and steering scripts. For reliability, I used matched prompt templates, multiple random seeds, randomized-direction and sham-intervention controls, grouped-bootstrap controls, and checked FP32 inference consistency with logit discrepancies below 4.2 × 10−5. I evaluated 40 natural-language responses and token-level generation trajectories, and the main conclusion was deliberately conservative: the behavior was too unstable to support a reliable causal circuit claim.

checks.label: Describe a time you worked with clinicians, scientists, or other non-technical subject matter experts on a research or data-analysis project. How did you translate their research needs into an analytical approach, and how did you communicate your findings back to them?
checks.expected: A clear example is my Research Assistant work at Columbia Zuckerman Institute on two-photon calcium-imaging data. The research problem was not just to build a model, but to evaluate whether self-supervised denoising improved reconstruction quality without sacrificing neuronal signal. I translated that into controlled analytical comparisons: four-direction spatial masking, PMD spatial-component selection, ResNet/U-Net/lightweight CNN configurations, Noise2Noise training-pair tests, and synthetic datasets with controlled noise levels. To make the results usable for scientists and wet-lab researchers, I reported trade-offs in signal retention, temporal correlation, reconstruction fidelity, and rank selection rather than only model metrics. I also organized the lab code into a downloadable package with public documentation and step-by-step guides, which is the same communication discipline I would bring to BCC’s clinical collaborators.
